title: Buckwheat as a summer cover crop
subtitle: A fast-growing annual that smothers weeds, feeds bees, and breaks down quickly.
excerpt: Buckwheat is a frost-tender annual grown in summer to cover bare soil, suppress weeds, and provide a short but intense flush of bee forage. Sow in May to July on any open bed and cut before it sets seed.
sourceNotes: Cover crop performance data from university extension services. Bee-forage value from Bumblebee Conservation Trust research. Frost tolerance data from standard UK horticultural reference.

glossaryTerms.definition: A dense, fast-growing cover crop grown specifically to shade out and suppress weed seedlings. Buckwheat, mustard, and phacelia are all used as smother crops in summer gaps between main-crop plantings.

content.text: Buckwheat is a fast-growing summer annual grown as a

between main-season plantings. It germinates and covers the ground in two to three weeks, crowds out annual weeds, and produces white flowers that bees work intensively. Cut it before seed sets and leave the material on the surface to break down.
Buckwheat is killed by any frost, so it is a summer-only crop. Do not sow before mid-May or later than mid-July if you want to cut it before the first autumn frosts arrive.
Sow seed 2 to 3 cm deep, broadcast over a raked bed. Aim for roughly 20 to 30 seeds per square metre. Germination takes five to seven days in warm weather. Water if the soil is dry at sowing.

Buckwheat reaches 30 to 50 cm in three to four weeks and begins to flower four to six weeks after sowing. Let it flower for two to three weeks before cutting, to give the bee forage time to run. Cut just as the first flowers fade and before any seed heads form. This keeps seed out of the soil.

Cut plants to the ground with shears or a scythe. Buckwheat stems are soft and break down in two to three weeks in warm weather. Spread the cut material in a thin, even layer across the bed so it does not form a mat. The bed will be ready to plant into within three to four weeks.

attrs.title: Buckwheat in a rotation
attrs.body: Buckwheat is most useful to fill the gap between main crops in midsummer. After early potatoes come out in July, sow buckwheat for six to eight weeks before planting an autumn brassica crop. After spring salads have finished in June, use buckwheat to hold the bed until a winter squash or leek goes in. The ground stays covered, weed-free, and active the whole time.
